meta.title_plain: Why a 1958 LEGO brick still clicks today
meta.teaser: Hot plastic, huge pressure and tiny precision make every LEGO brick fit perfectly.

page.title: Why a 1958 LEGO brick still clicks today
page.sub: The story of how a LEGO brick is made
page.bigIdea: Every LEGO brick is made with super-tiny precision, so a brick from 1958 still fits one made this morning.

cards.title: Tiny grains, giant silos
cards.front: Every brick starts as plastic smaller than a pea.
cards.back: Trucks deliver colourful plastic grains called granules. Giant hoses suck them into silos three storeys high. Each silo holds up to 33 tonnes.
cards.tryit: Build the tallest silo you can from 20 bricks in 10 minutes. Can it hold a minifigure on top?

cards.title: Melt, squeeze, cool, pop
cards.front: A brick is born in about 10 seconds.
cards.back: Machines heat the plastic to about 230°C until it's like goo. They squeeze it into a metal mould, cool it, then pop the brick out.
cards.tryit: Count how many bricks you can click together in 10 seconds. A machine makes a brick in that time.

cards.title: Precise to a hair
cards.front: Why do bricks grip so perfectly?
cards.back: Moulds are accurate to about a tenth of a hair's width. Too loose and bricks fall apart. Too tight and you couldn't pull them off.
cards.tryit: Build a 2x4 tower ten bricks high, then pull it apart. Feel that perfect grip, called clutch power.

cards.title: The 1958 promise
cards.front: Old bricks and new bricks are best friends.
cards.back: LEGO filed the patent for today's brick on 28 January 1958. The stud size and spacing never changed, so 1958 bricks still click with new ones.
cards.tryit: Find your oldest and newest bricks. Build a tiny 'time bridge' that joins them in 5 minutes.

cards.title: Robots, printers and checks
cards.front: What happens after a brick pops out?
cards.back: Robot trucks carry full boxes away. Printers add faces and details. Only about 18 bricks in every million fail the quality check.
cards.tryit: Be a quality inspector: sort 30 bricks by colour in 5 minutes and spot any scratched ones.

quiz.q: Why do bricks made in 1958 still click with new ones?
opts: The stud size and spacing never changed
quiz.hint: Think about what has to match for two bricks to click.
quiz.why: LEGO kept the same measurements since 1958, so every brick fits every other brick.

quiz.q: What would happen if a mould were a tiny bit too big?
opts: Bricks would be loose and fall apart
quiz.hint: Imagine a stud that is slightly bigger than the hole it goes into, or smaller.
quiz.why: Even a tiny size change breaks the grip, which is why moulds are so precise.

quiz.q: Which order is right for making a brick?
quiz.hint: The plastic has to be soft before it can take a new shape.
quiz.why: Granules are melted, squeezed into the mould, then cooled so the brick keeps its shape.

quiz.q: LEGO makes about 36 billion pieces a year. About how many is that per second?
quiz.hint: A year has about 31 million seconds. Try dividing.
quiz.why: 36 billion divided by about 31.5 million seconds is roughly 1,140 pieces every second.
